papers.title: Changes in the wing spot pattern of the endangered butterfly Phengaris teleius thirty years after its reintroduction
papers.abstract: 1. Reintroduced insect populations founded by few individuals can change in phenotype through founder effects, genetic drift and new environmental conditions. Butterfly wing spot patterns, their fluctuating asymmetry and their variability can reflect such changes and population stress. 2. We studied the spot pattern of the hindwing underside of 267 Phengaris teleius butterflies from the Polish source metapopulation at the time of their reintroduction to the Netherlands in 1990, and from the current Polish and Dutch metapopulations (2019-2020). We analysed the presence, size, asymmetry and fusion of the spots, and the shape and variability of the spot pattern. 3. The reintroduced Dutch metapopulation differed in spot pattern shape from both Polish ones and was less variable than the source metapopulation. The two Polish metapopulations did not differ from each other in shape. Dutch butterflies also had a more frequent spot 11 than the current Polish metapopulation and a larger spot 1 than the source ones, and the concordance between both wings in the presence of the facultative spots differed among metapopulations, being lowest in the Dutch one. Only the presence of spot 10 in females and spot fusion in males changed in the Polish metapopulation between 1990 and 2019. 4. These results agree with the founder effect and the loss of genetic variability after the reintroduction, although local adaptation or plasticity cannot be ruled out. Although based on a single reintroduction, these results suggest that spot pattern variability, measured from photographs, could complement the genetic monitoring of reintroduced insect populations.

papers.title: Environmental Noise and Lag Select Distinct Phenotypic Bet Hedging in Microbial Metabolic Allocation
papers.abstract: Genetically identical microbial cells often differ in their growth rate and metabolic state, and in how long they take to resume growth after a shift of conditions. Preparing for uncertain future conditions is costly: cells that allocate part of their proteome to a future nutrient grow more slowly on the present one. Bet hedging offers a complementary strategy: a genotype whose cells occupy different metabolic states makes it likely that some of them are suited to whatever condition follows and resume growth quickly. Here, we investigate when phenotypic variability in metabolic allocation can outperform the evolutionary stable homogeneous strategy, in which all cells share the same allocation. We consider serial-dilution cultures, where each cycle ends when the nutrient is exhausted, and fluctuations in dilution or nutrient supply change the fold increase in biomass required in each cycle, i.e., the growth factor. We identify two distinct mechanisms by which selection can favor phenotypic heterogeneity. First, noise in the growth factor leaves the optimal mean allocation unchanged but can destabilize the homogeneous strategy: cycles that demand much growth favor fast growers, whereas cycles that demand little growth favor well-prepared cells. Variability in allocation is therefore favored above a critical noise level, set by the mean logarithm of the growth factor and by how steeply the lag increases as the allocation to the incoming nutrient decreases. Second, with multiple possible future nutrients, different cells can allocate their proteome to different future nutrients. When the lag is sufficiently long relative to the growth time, an all-in strategy, in which cells specialize in individual future nutrients, is favored independently of noise in the growth factor. Invasion analysis of narrow phenotypic distributions shows that these two mechanisms define four evolutionary regimes, confirmed by competition and evolution simulations. Our results show how environmental uncertainty can make cell-to-cell variability selectively advantageous, so that evolution acts on the distribution of phenotypes within a genotype, not only on its mean.

papers.title: EpiCycle: A flexible approach for scalable, three-dimensional reconstructions of complex epithelial tissues
papers.abstract: Understanding organ development and repair requires methods to precisely describe cell geometry. Recent image analysis methods allow increasingly accurate segmentation of simple epithelial tissues. However, many vertebrate organs contain more complex stratified epithelia, for which accurate 3D cellular segmentation remains challenging. Here, we describe EpiCycle, an iterative, user-friendly approach developed to address the unique segmentation challenges posed by stratified epithelia. Starting from sparse or no ground truth annotations, EpiCycle guides users through a human-in-the-loop refinement process that culminates in 3D consensus reconstruction. Through cyclical correction, annotation and model retraining, EpiCycle allows users to progressively build robust, dataset-specific segmentation models while simultaneously generating 3D ground truth. To highlight the utility of EpiCycle, we train models that generate high-confidence, tissue-level segmentation of the stratified squamous epithelium in adult zebrafish skin. We apply our approach to segmentation of mouse embryonic branching salivary glands demonstrating its versatility across organs and species. Finally, we produce and analyze quantitative measurements of stratified cell geometry in human fetal epidermis. Thus, EpiCycle enables scalable and quantitative 3D reconstructions of complex vertebrate tissues without relying on pre-existing ground truth.

papers.title: HDAC6 inhibition rewires carbon metabolism to expose an asparagine dependency in multiple myeloma.
papers.abstract: Multiple myeloma (MM) remains a challenging malignancy with limited therapeutic options upon relapse/refractory disease, necessitating novel combination strategies. Malignant plasma cells sustain continuous immunoglobulin production, a biosynthetic and secretory burden that places heavy demand on central carbon metabolism and creates potentially targetable metabolic vulnerabilities. Previously, we found a role for HDAC6 in modulating glycolytic metabolism. Our goal here was to find induced metabolic vulnerabilities that could be targeted after HDAC6 inhibition or knockdown. Genetic silencing of HDAC6 or pharmacological inhibition with the selective inhibitor BAS-2, suppressed glycolytic flux, reduced pyruvate and lactate labelling from 13C6-glucose, and remodeled mitochondrial morphology in MM cell lines. Global proteomic analysis revealed coordinated upregulation of amino acid transporters (SLC3A2, SLC7A1, SLC1A5, SLC7A5), and spent-medium measurements confirmed an increased depletion of extracellular amino acids. Collectively, this data indicates that BAS-2-treated cells increased their dependence on amino acid import. To identify essential amino acids, we screened MM cells treated with BAS-2 and individually depleted each of the 20 proteinogenic amino acids. Upon depletion of either asparagine, arginine, or aspartate enhanced BAS-2 induced cell death. Combination treatment of BAS-2 and the FDA-approved drug L-asparaginase (L-ASNase), which depletes asparagine, demonstrated synergistic cytotoxicity across a panel of MM cell lines. The combination treatment induces a reliance on asparagine synthesis from pyruvate, as identified by labelling from 13C6-glucose-glucose. Mechanistically the combination induced inhibition of protein synthesis, activated the integrated stress response, and increased ATF4 and CHOP protein expression. Lastly, we showed in vivo in the chick chorioallantoic membrane (CAM) model that BAS-2 and L-ASNase reduced tumour volume and CD138 positivity. In summary, these findings establish HDAC6 inhibition as a translatable metabolic target which rewires amino acid import that can be exploited with L-ASNase in MM.

papers.title: Stromal mitochondrial reprogramming and transfer reveal a chemotherapy-associated tumor state in ovarian cancer
papers.abstract: Mitochondrial transfer from stromal cells promotes ovarian cancer progression, yet the functional state of donor mitochondria remains poorly understood. Here we define a stress-adapted mitochondrial state in carcinoma-associated mesenchymal stem cells (CA-MSCs), characterized by increased respiratory and glycolytic activity despite increased mitochondrial proton leak and inefficient coupling of respiration to ATP production, oxidative stress, and elevated mitochondrial DNA variant burden. We identify WT1 as a regulator of mitochondrial reprogramming and PDK4 as a metabolic adaptation critical for CA-MSC growth. We further show that CA-MSCs preferentially transfer highly oxidized mitochondria to ovarian cancer cells. In a freshly-dissociated primary high grade serous ovarian cancer patient tumor, using mitochondrial variant tracking, we identify a transcriptionally distinct tumor population sharing mitochondrial variant patterns with stroma, in line with stromal-tumor mitochondrial transfer. This transcriptional signature is enriched in residual tumors following chemotherapy across four independent patient cohorts. Together, these findings establish stromal mitochondrial reprogramming and the preferential transfer of oxidatively-stressed mitochondria as important features of ovarian cancer heterogeneity and persistence following chemotherapy.

papers.title: A gene-edited chicken model of ocular coloboma reveals Netrin-1 is required for pioneer cell detachment during optic fissure closure
papers.abstract: Coloboma, a leading cause of childhood blindness, results from failed OFC. Variants in NTN1 (Netrin-1) are linked to coloboma and other tissue fusion defects, but how Netrin-1 influences epithelial fusion is unknown. We generated a germline NTN1 knockout chicken and analysed the fissure margins by immunofluorescence, in situ hybridisation, single-nucleus RNA sequencing and micro-CT. NTN1-/- embryos developed highly penetrant bilateral colobomas. The basement membrane (BM) was remodelled normally, yet pioneer cells at the optic fissure margins (OFMs) failed to detach and mix across the midline, retaining apical actin and displaying increased cadherin at the fissure edges. The ventral neural retina showed reduced apoptosis and became overgrown and folded at the fissure edges. These data show that Netrin-1 is required for pioneer cell detachment and this process is independent of BM remodelling. We found that pioneer cells in wild type (WT) OFMs were transiently exposed to fibronectin-rich periocular mesenchyme (POM) during BM remodelling, with fibronectin and laminin fragments localised at their exposed edges. Netrin-1 reduced adhesion of HEK293 cells to fibronectin in vitro, with and without laminin, but not to laminin alone, suggesting Netrin-1 mediates a substrate specific effect on cell adhesion. ITGB8 and ITGAV were co-expressed with NTN1 in pioneer cells, and Netrin-1 co-immunoprecipitated with ITGB8, identifying integrin V{beta}8 as a candidate Netrin-1 receptor in OFC. Integrin V{beta}8 with fibronectin typically activate canonical TGF{beta} signalling, however we found pSMAD2 was specifically absent from pioneer cell nuclei during fusion. In contrast, phosphorylated FAK was present in WT but not mutant fissures, indicating that Netrin-1 activates integrin mediated focal adhesion signalling in OFC. We propose that Netrin-1 and V{beta}8 enable pioneer cells to respond to transient POM-derived cues, such as fibronectin, triggering detachment and initiating fusion. This proposed mechanism could explain a direct role for the POM in mediating OFC.

papers.title: Transient telomerase mRNA delivery extends the proliferative capacity of patient-derived Duchenne muscular dystrophy myogenic progenitors
papers.abstract: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is an X-linked disease, characterised by progressive skeletal and cardiac muscle degeneration and impaired regeneration. Repeated regenerative cycles contribute to muscle stem cell exhaustion, potentially driven by telomere shortening under chronic proliferative demand. Here, we tested whether transient delivery of hTERT mRNA can increase the relative telomere signal (Q-FISH) in patient-derived DMD myogenic progenitors (CD56+) and interstitial (CD56-) cells from two DMD donors, compared with one control donor. hTERT mRNA treatment increased the relative telomere signal and added 2 to 6 population doublings in DMD myogenic progenitors, whereas healthy donor cells showed no comparable benefit in proliferation. Exploratory transcriptomic analysis indicated genotype-associated differences in translation- and cell-cycle-related gene sets following hTERT treatment. Telomere elongation and improved proliferation were not accompanied by recovery of myogenic differentiation; no karyotypic abnormalities were detected under the conditions tested. By transiently increasing the proliferative output of dystrophic cells without genomic integration, this proof of concept provides a basis for further investigation of telomere-associated proliferative limits in DMD and a starting point for future regenerative approaches.

papers.title: Rare Epithelial Sentinel Cells Establish Functional Domains of the Airway
papers.abstract: Organs exposed to the environment must sense threats in order to evoke protective physiologic responses. Recent single-cell sequencing studies of the airway epithelium have led to the identification of a suite of rare epithelial cells, many of which are unified by their ability to sense stimuli1,2. Herein, we explore how organized networks of epithelial sentinel cells transduce distinct stimuli to alter tissue function by employing a combination of cell type-specific calcium indicators, optogenetics, chemogenetics, cell ablation, and live ACh and ATP sensors. We define a new diversity of functional sentinel cells including 3 new subtypes of chemosensory tuft cells. We further show that solitary neuroendocrine cells, like their tuft cell counterparts, generate stimulus-induced waves of calcium activation. These waves originate from a central sentinel cell and expand outwards to encompass a circular domain of surrounding epithelial cells. We demonstrate that basolateral secretion and diffusion of neurotransmitters cause the activation of the surrounding epithelial effector cells including basal stem cells which were not previously known to be participants in sentinel cell-induced calcium waves. We show that these diffusion-limited domains (DLDs) are generated by specific patterns of ACh and ATP secretion characteristic of specific sentinel cell populations. The speed, intensity, and domain size of DLDs are dictated by the degree of stimulus-triggered neurotransmitter secretion. Thus, DLDs represent a unified mechanism for specifying functional domains within the airway epithelium. Triggered sentinel cells generate surrounding circular domains of increased mucociliary transport and enhance stem cell replication. Insulated sentinel cell networks are tuned to distinct stimuli. Sentinel cells are distributed in sufficient numbers to ensure comprehensive epithelial coverage. However, the amplitude and number of DLDs scale with stimulus intensity, permitting both local and global physiologic activation of the epithelium. Additionally, the distribution of sentinel cells can vary with organ anatomy, resulting in compartmentalized physiologic responses. Furthermore, cytokines modulate DLD responses. IL-1{beta} amplifies ciliary action by generating larger and more intense DLDs, while IFN-{gamma} reduces the density of DLDs by directly depleting sentinel cells. Finally, we show that a fungal metabolite triggers DLDs. In aggregate, we reveal a sophisticated collective of diverse sentinel cells that activate surrounding circular domains of airway epithelium to generate protective responses to environmental threats.

papers.title: Time-resolved multi-omics reveals constitutive defense preparedness and early responses to soybean cyst nematode in wild soybean
papers.abstract: Soybean (Glycine max), a versatile cash crop, is the largest global source of plant-based protein and second-largest source of vegetable oil. However, soybean cyst nematode (SCN; Heterodera glycines) is the most economically damaging pest of soybean worldwide, causing substantial yield losses annually. Currently, the effectiveness of widely deployed genetic resistance in soybean cultivars is increasingly challenged by evolving SCN populations; therefore, identifying new sources and mechanisms of SCN resistance is critical. Crop wild relatives, the ancestral or closely related wild species of domesticated crops, are rich sources of genetic diversity encompassing various beneficial traits, including pathogen resistance. In this study, we applied a comparative, multi-omics approach to examine the molecular mechanisms underlying SCN resistance in wild soybean (Glycine soja). We integrated transcriptomic, metabolomic, and proteomic data from two wild soybean genotypes representing contrasting responses to SCN (S54, resistant; S67, susceptible) at early- and late-stage infection. Our results reveal distinct constitutive molecular profiles and contrasting genotype-specific responses to SCN infection. The resistant genotype S54 exhibited a stronger early transcriptional response, particularly involving defense signaling and stress-responsive processes, whereas the susceptible genotype S67 showed a delayed response. Gene co-expression and integrative multi-omics analyses identified coordinated molecular networks associated with resistance, including defense-related genes and metabolic features. Together, these findings suggest that SCN resistance in wild soybean involves both pre-existing molecular differences and early activation of defense-associated responses. Our work identifies candidate genes, metabolites, and pathways for future functional testing. Ultimately, these findings provide an integrated multi-omics view of SCN resistance mechanisms in wild soybean, extending our understanding beyond commonly studied cultivar-based resistance and offering potential targets for soybean improvement.

papers.title: Trade-offs between sexual and clonal reproduction differ within versus among populations
papers.abstract: Plants exhibit large variation in reproductive strategies, from obligately sexual to exclusively asexual. Clonal vegetative reproduction is common among plants, and despite theory assuming that trade-offs exist between sexual and clonal reproduction, empirical demonstrations of trade-offs remain elusive. Here we examined whether the strength of genotypic trade-offs in white clover (Trifolium repens) depends on spatial scale of sampling, and the environmental factors that favour sexual versus clonal reproduction. We quantified genetic variation and tested for trade-offs within and among populations from North America. Within a population, we grew up to 5 clonal replicates from each of 38 genotypes collected from a population in southern Canada. Among populations, we grew up to 5 clonal replicates from each of 46 populations, collected from a 21{o} transect from southern USA to northern Canada. All plants were randomized in a single growth chamber and grown for 12 weeks while keeping resource availability constant. From each plant, we measured investment in sexual reproduction as the number of inflorescences, and investment in clonal reproduction as the number of stolons, total stolon length and leaf area. We also extracted multiple environmental variables from each population. There was substantial genetic variation for all traits at both spatial scales, but genetic variation was always greater among populations. At the within population scale, the number of inflorescences was positively genetically correlated with the number of stolons and leaf area. Among populations, the number of inflorescences was negatively genetically correlated with both stolon length and leaf area. Colder, drier, high-latitude sites were associated with increased clonality. Our results show that the strength and direction of genotypic trade-offs differs within versus among populations, with trade-offs only being apparent at the largest scale among populations. These results provide insight into when and how trade-offs evolve between sexual and clonal plant reproductive strategies.

papers.title: A human-accelerated enhancer rewires FOXC1-dependent skeletal development
papers.abstract: The evolution of human skeletal morphology involved modifications to conserved developmental programs, but the underlying regulatory mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here we integrate single-cell transcriptomic atlases of developing human, macaque and mouse limbs with comparative chromatin interaction maps of chondrocytes. We identify human-biased transcriptional programs within conserved osteochondral lineages and link divergent chromatin interactions to human-specific sequence changes. These analyses identify zooHAR.30, a human accelerated region that contacts the promoter of FOXC1, a key regulator of skeletal development. Human-specific substitutions within zooHAR.30 alter transcription factor binding, and the human sequence exhibits enhanced regulatory activity in chondrocytes and more spatially restricted activity in the developing limb, predominantly in the zeugopod, compared with the chimpanzee ortholog. Replacing the endogenous human sequence with its chimpanzee ortholog reduces FOXC1 and GMDS expression, impairs cell proliferation and osteochondral differentiation, and alters FOXC1 occupancy across skeletal regulatory elements, including a GDF5 enhancer implicated in knee morphology and osteoarthritis. Our findings reveal how evolutionary changes in a single enhancer can propagate through a conserved developmental regulatory network, providing a mechanistic link between human-specific sequence divergence and the evolution of skeletal developmental programs.

papers.title: High-resolution cryo-EM of ribosomes in mammalian neurons
papers.abstract: Brain function depends on protein synthesis (translation), which controls neurodevelopment, synaptic plasticity, and memory formation. To understand the molecular mechanisms of translational control, the functional states of neuronal ribosomes must be determined. We visualized the translational apparatus within induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSC)-derived human neurons and in human and mouse neuron-derived lysates, using cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) with high-resolution 2D template matching (2DTM) and large-area imaging (DeCo-LACE). Cryo-EM maps at up to 2.6 [A] resolution reveal structural details of numerous functional states of ribosomes. Initiating 40S subunits abundantly feature initiation factor eIF1S (also known as 5MP) indicating a tight control of translation initiation. Ribosomes with elongation factors comprise ~90% of 80S particles, suggesting a high prevalence of translating ribosomes. Most elongating ribosomes sample pre-decoding states with aminoacyl-tRNA*eEF1A*GTP and a well-resolved decoding center prior to aminoacyl-tRNA acceptance. On the large ribosomal subunit, a conserved loop of uL16 stabilizes the CCA end of peptidyl-tRNA, suggesting a ribosomal protein contribution into RNA-catalyzed peptidyl transfer. The composition of peripheral ribosomal proteins, including the P-stalk proteins proposed to be substoichiometric in neurons, is homogeneous throughout ribosome states. The compositional heterogeneity of ribosomes is therefore negligible or only occurs under specific cellular conditions. Our work provides a comprehensive visualization of ribosome states within neurons and paves the way for probing translation regulation and dysregulation in neurological diseases using cryo-EM.

papers.title: Advancing Cyanobacterial Toxin Monitoring Capacity: A Large-Scale Multi-Year Comparison of ELISA, LC-MS/MS, and qPCR in Temperate Waters
papers.abstract: Cyanobacterial toxins are an increasing environmental and public health concern, driven by rising temperatures and anthropogenic pressures such as eutrophication. Due to the colder climate, Northern Europe is generally believed to be less vulnerable, however, cyanobacterial blooms have increased in recent years in many areas including Arctic lakes and Northern Baltic Sea. Yet, monitoring remains challenging due to toxin diversity, variable bloom dynamics, and the differences in analytical targets among methods. We compared the complementarity, agreement, and practical utility of enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS), and quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) for detecting cyanobacterial toxins and toxin-producing genotypes. This large-scale, multi-season study leveraged a sampling effort encompassing over 816 samples from freshwater, brackish, and marine ecosystems across Sweden over three consecutive summers. Toxins detected included microcystins, nodularin, cylindrospermopsins, anatoxins, and saxitoxins; where the fraction found in the cyanobacteria or as dissolved toxins varied with toxin type. Overall, concentrations measured using the three methods were proportional, but ELISA yielded, on average, approximately three times higher values than LC-MS/MS. ELISA provided high-throughput with lower selectivity compared to LC-MS/MS that ensured congener specific confirmation while qPCR complementarily revealed widespread presence of toxin-gene-carrying cyanobacteria. Across the 173 triple-analyzed samples, the combined use of ELISA, LC-MS/MS, and qPCR improved interpretation of cyanotoxin occurrence, bloom stage and potential risk compared to any single method alone. This multi-season field study represents one of the most extensive evaluations of these methods applied for cyanobacteria and their toxins in temperate waters.

papers.title: Structures of human adenoviruses D36 and D56 provide insights into adenovirus diversity and cement protein networks
papers.abstract: 83 out of 118 human adenoviruses (HAdVs) belong to species D, which includes respiratory viruses, recombinants associated with rare, fatal neonatal infections, and viruses developed as vectors for clinical applications. The structural basis for variability in capsid-host interactions, and the complex network of cement proteins stabilizing the inner face of the capsids are incompletely understood. We report cryo-EM structures of HAdV-D36 and HAdV-D56 at 2.5 and 2.6 A resolution, respectively. Capsid surface features are well resolved, allowing structural comparisons of hypervariable regions. A near-complete assignment of inner cement proteins reveals novel capsid interactions for proteins IIIa, VI, VII, and VIII, the last of which is assigned to a conserved, hexon-interacting peptide previously thought to be protein V. These near-complete maps of two HAdV-D capsids may inform vector design and provide a reference for the role of individual proteins in virion assembly and disassembly.

papers.title: Viral-bacterial arms race in the marine sponge Halichondria panicea
papers.abstract: Sponges are complex holobionts/metaorganisms and important models for host-microbe interactions, yet their viral communities remain poorly understood. Here, we characterized the diversity of viruses associated with the marine sponge Halichondria panicea from different locations in the North Atlantic and Baltic Sea. Most sponge-associated viruses were also detected in the surrounding seawater, while little evidence was found for a shared sponge-specific core virome across locations. A subset of viruses that were enriched in sponges over seawater was explored further. Its functional potential included diverse auxiliary genes of metabolic functions, particularly nucleotide and cofactor metabolism, as well as bacterial cell surface modification. At the community level, the predicted viral anti-defenses broadly correspond to the predicted microbial defense classes, suggesting an evolutionary arms race between viruses and their microbial hosts within the sponge holobiont. Furthermore, the diverse defense systems identified on the genomes of the dominant bacterial symbiont "Candidatus Halichondribacter symbioticus", together with variation in defense gene content and sequence, suggest that viruses contribute to genomic diversification of the major sponge symbiont. Finally, a gene transfer agent was identified on the genome of "Ca. H. symbioticus", which represents a mechanism for horizontal gene transfer and DNA exchange within this symbiont population. Overall, our results indicate that viruses are dynamic components of the H. panicea microbiome and contribute to genome diversification of the main sponge symbiont "Ca. H. symbioticus".

papers.title: Deciphering the synthetic route and apoptotic mechanisms of oxime ester (UAH-4): A potent ursolic acid derivative targeting colorectal cancer
papers.abstract: The study aimed to synthesize a novel derivative of ursolic acid (UA) and evaluate its anticancer efficacy against Colorectal Cancer (CRC) cells, with a focus on elucidating its mechanism of action. The derivative, UAH-4, was synthesized through a multi-step chemical process and characterized using spectroscopic techniques. In vitro cytotoxicity of UAH-4 was assessed using the SRB assay, while its impact on colony formation, cell migration, Reactive Oxygen Species (ROS) generation, Mitochondrial Membrane Potential (MMP) loss, and nuclear morphology were evaluated. Western blotting was performed to investigate the induction of apoptosis by UAH-4. UAH-4 exhibited significant cytotoxicity against various cancer cell lines, with a notable impact on the HCT-116 cancer cell line. The compound disrupted colony formation and inhibited cell migration, suggesting potential anti-metastatic effects. Mechanistic investigations revealed UAH-4-induced alterations in nuclear morphology, reactive oxygen species generation, loss of mitochondrial membrane potential, and apoptosis in HCT-116 cells. The study demonstrates the potent anticancer activity of UAH-4 against colorectal cancer cells through the induction of apoptosis. These findings suggest that UAH-4 holds promise as a therapeutic agent for CRC and warrants further investigation for its clinical potential in cancer therapy.

papers.title: Slow mitochondria, long life: a phylogenetic comparative analysis in 41 avian species
papers.abstract: Mitochondrial aerobic metabolism is thought to play a central role in the mechanisms underlying aging. However, because metabolism scales with body mass, which strongly predicts lifespan, disentangling the relationship between mitochondrial metabolism and lifespan from the shared allometric scaling of both traits with body mass remains a persistent challenge. Here, we address this issue by using a phylogenetically controlled, multivariate Bayesian approach to test whether different mitochondrial traits covary with lifespan independently of body mass, across 41 bird species (maximal lifespan: 6-41 years; body mass: 9 g-13 kg). Our results show that, after controlling for body mass, species maximal lifespan was associated with the cellular control of mitochondrial respiration: longer-lived species showed lower respiration under native cellular conditions (i.e. ROUTINE), but not at maximum fluxes (i.e. OXPHOS). Therefore, longer-lived species used a smaller proportion of their maximal capacity, indicating a larger spare respiratory capacity. Phylogenetic signal was moderate across the four respiration rates, and although mitochondrial traits were tightly correlated within individuals, they showed little evidence of coordinated evolutionary change across species. These results suggest that, in birds, lifespan is linked to how mitochondrial activity is regulated relative to capacity, rather than to maximal performance or efficiency per se, and point to the cellular control of mitochondrial respiration as a potential mechanism underlying the evolution of lifespan.

papers.title: Genomic signatures of cognitive evolution in birds
papers.abstract: The ability to invent novel behavioral solutions was a crucial factor in the success of Homo species. Beyond humans, high levels of innovation have evolved independently across several animal lineages, including birds. Birds provide a particularly striking example, with highly innovative species distributed across multiple clades, creating an opportunity to investigate whether independent origins of this phenotype involve recurring evolutionary mechanisms. To investigate the genomic basis of avian innovativeness, we analyzed high-quality long-read genomes from a broad sampling of avian species, leveraging recent genomic resources from the Vertebrate Genomes Project. To investigate both lineage-specific molecular changes and broader genomic correlates of innovativeness, we analyzed coding sequences in selected clades where highly innovative species occur among less innovative relatives, and examined the evolutionary rates of conserved non-exonic elements (CNEEs) across the avian phylogeny using innovation as a continuous trait. We identified candidate genes under recurrent positive selection, including those implicated in neural development and function, as well as maternal nutrient provisioning to developing embryos. In parallel, CNEEs overlapping differentially accessible regions in glial cells and specific glutamatergic neuronal population of the avian pallium showed stronger evolutionary constraint in more innovative lineages. Together, these findings link the evolution of avian innovativeness across distinct branches of the avian phylogeny to molecular changes spanning neural function, early developmental processes, and the regulation of gene activity in specific pallial cell populations.

papers.title: Spiny mice are resistant to retinal fibrosis and display a capacity for ganglion cell recovery after NMDA-induced injury
papers.abstract: Degenerative eye diseases affect millions of people and can ultimately lead to blindness. Facilitating regeneration of retinal neurons in mammals could prevent or slow vision loss. Spiny mice (genus Acomys) display remarkable regenerative abilities across many tissues, including the spinal cord. Utilizing the neurotoxin NMDA to damage inner retinal neurons, we assessed the response to retinal damage in Acomys using the well documented response of Mus musculus as a baseline for comparison. In response to acute retinal damage, two waves of cell proliferation were detected in Acomys: the first wave (1-4 dpi) mostly consisted of proliferating microglia, whereas the second wave (6-21 dpi) included microglia and Muller glia. Reactive gliosis was significantly reduced in Acomys compared to Mus, with minimal expression of acute gliotic markers such as GFAP and NES after injury. In Acomys retinas, proliferating microglia of various activation states were observed weeks after injury, whereas in Mus, the microglia returned to a resting state by 10 dpi. Additionally, by 121 dpi, recovery of RBPMS+ ganglion cells was detected in Acomys, a small number of which were also positive for EdU, suggesting they were derived from proliferating cells. Taken together, our results show that the retinal damage response in Acomys features an initial burst of microglial proliferation, followed by some Muller glial proliferation, reduced reactive gliosis, and RGC recovery. As such, these findings create a novel opportunity to explore potential mechanisms of retinal repair and neural recovery in mammals.

papers.title: A Tunable Centromere-inheritance Switch Links DNA Replication to Germline Regeneration and Reproductive Aging
papers.abstract: Centromeres direct chromosome segregation and are defined not by DNA sequence but by CENP-A-containing chromatin, raising the question of how centromeric identity is faithfully transmitted through DNA replication, and whether this process influences stem cell behavior. In the Drosophila male germline, germline stem cells (GSCs) assemble asymmetric sister centromeres linked to non-random sister-chromatid segregation, but how this asymmetry is established and whether it contributes to germline function remain unclear. Using high-resolution microscopy on cell-type and stage-specific chromatin fibers, we show that pre-existing CENP-A (CID in flies) is recycled asymmetrically onto newly replicated sister centromeres in early germ cells including GSCs, while differentiating progenitors redistribute CID nearly symmetrically. Inner kinetochore component CENP-C shows a similar pattern, with both proteins enriched on the lagging strand. The CID chaperone CAL1 associates with centromeres during S phase and is required for this asymmetric incorporation of both CID and CENP-C and for normal germline function; compromising CAL1 leads to either early-germline tumors or germ cell loss. Intriguingly, reducing lagging-strand Primase 1, a component of the DNA polymerase (Pol) complex, is sufficient to induce sister centromere asymmetry in differentiating progenitors, promoting a stem cell-like centromere state, proper centrosome orientation, and niche-directed microtubule behavior during dedifferentiation of progenitors. Combining modest CID overexpression with Primase 1 reduction further enhances dedifferentiation and redifferentiation, significantly improving male fertility during aging and regeneration following {gamma}-irradiation. Together, these findings identify that replication-coupled, strand-biased centromere inheritance can be tuned to regulate cellular plasticity, linking DNA replication to regenerative capacity and reproductive fitness.

papers.title: Transgene-free immortalisation of bovine satellite cells by genetic disruption of CDKN2A
papers.abstract: Production of cultivated meat demands a supply of cells that differentiate into muscle, even after extended proliferation. As primary bovine satellite cells (PrimSCs) lose proliferation and differentiation capacity over prolonged culture, immortalised cell lines are necessary for rapid commercialisation. Here, we report the first evidence of a transgene-free single knockout mRNA-hit-and-run-based strategy that yields immortalised bovine satellite cells (ImmSCs). We demonstrate targeted disruption of CDKN2A alone is sufficient to immortalise SCs from three cow breeds. ImmSCs maintained a 17h doubling time over 75 population doublings, while sustaining myogenic potential in 2D and 3D differentiation. Transcriptionally, ImmSCs evade senescence and continue to resemble young primary cells. Finally, we show that ImmSCs are non-tumorigenic and proliferate even with a 90% reduction in FGF-2, HGF, and T3. By combining immortalisation with regulatory compatibility, we demonstrate a simple and generalisable single-locus disruption strategy that minimizes batch variability and enables scalable production of cultivated meat.

papers.title: A novel simultaneous RNA extraction workflow from mouse Retinal Pigmented Epithelial (RPE) and retina
papers.abstract: Purpose: In Posterior Segment Eye Diseases (PSEDs), the homeostatic relation between retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and retina is disrupted. A better understanding of the transcriptomic changes occurring in different ocular cell types can help to elucidate disease mechanisms. Currently, there is no complete detailed workflow describing the process of simultaneous RNA isolation from RPE and retina separately. In this paper, our aim was to develop an easy, reproducible protocol for simultaneous isolation of RNA from both murine RPE and retina. Methods: We developed an efficient and straightforward workflow for isolating RNA from both murine RPE and retina simultaneously. We described the method in detail spanning from mouse euthanasia to downstream RNA analysis. We compared the efficiency of this isolation method between different mice strains (C57BL/6 vs BALB/c). Results: Our method provided high yield of RNA from both RPE and retina across different strains. We observed better quality of RPE RNA in terms of A260/130 ratios in C57BL/6 mice. The retinal RNA quality and yield were comparable across both strains. Beta-catenin immunofluorescent staining also validated our success of RPE removal in the choroidal flat-mounts in both strains. Conclusions: We described an improved workflow for obtaining RNA simultaneously from both RPE and retina. We compared the efficiency of our process via multitude of downstream analyses across different mice strains. Translational Relevance: This method will be beneficial to understand the RPE or retinal tissue specific mRNA transcript changes in preclinical mice models of PSEDs.

papers.title: Hepatocyte NMD restrains inflammation and is impaired in alcohol-associated hepatitis
papers.abstract: Nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) limits the abundance of transcripts containing premature termination codons (PTCs) and regulates other endogenous mRNAs. How distinct transcripts respond to reduced NMD capacity in liver disease remains poorly understood. Here, we found that hepatic UPF1 and UPF2 protein abundance was markedly reduced in human alcohol-associated hepatitis. Hepatocyte-specific Upf2 deletion in mice caused liver injury, cell death, and macrophage accumulation, with innate immune gene induction evident by day 11. Integrated intron-exon RNA-seq analysis identified 259 protein-coding candidate NMD-regulated genes, including genes involved in inflammation, stress responses, and metabolism. Canonical NMD substrates, including the PTC-containing isoforms of Tra2b, Hnrnpl, and Ptbp2, accumulated markedly following hepatocyte-specific Upf2 deletion. In contrast, partial Upf2 knockdown in primary mouse hepatocytes induced NMD-targeted inflammatory genes, including Ccl2, Ccl7, Icam1, and Ifit2 while producing only modest changes in the examined PTC-containing isoforms. Human alcohol-associated hepatitis livers likewise exhibited increased CCL2, ICAM1, and IFIT2 expression, accompanied by modest and variable changes in these canonical NMD substrates. These findings support differential transcript responsiveness to reduced NMD capacity and indicate that selected PTC-containing substrates may incompletely reflect its effects on endogenous gene regulation. Together, our results identify hepatocyte NMD as a restraint on inflammatory gene expression and suggest that its suppression may contribute to hepatic inflammation in alcohol-associated hepatitis.

papers.title: The thylakoid K+ exchange antiporter KEA3 affects NPQ dynamics and growth in the green algae Chlamydomonas reinhardtii
papers.abstract: The highly variable environmental conditions that photosynthetic organism experience in nature require rapid and long-term acclimatory responses. Light and CO2 availability are tightly linked within the cell. When light intensity rises, CO2 fixation accelerates, causing intracellular CO2 to become limiting for photosynthesis. Nonphotochemical quenching (NPQ) mechanisms prevent over excitation of the photosynthetic electron transport chain and consequent damage by reactive oxygen species. Energy dependent quenching (qE) is the fastest NPQ component and responds to thylakoid lumen acidification, a consequence of photosynthesis limiting CO2 concentrations. In vascular plants, the thylakoid K/H antiporter KEA3 is required for qE downregulation after a high to low light transition, transiently enhancing photosynthetic quantum yield. Here, we demonstrate that the same holds for the unicellular green alga Chlamydomonas reinhardtii (Cr). Unlike vascular plants, CrKEA3 also contributes to qE relaxation in the dark and influences growth. The crkea3 mutants from higher light intensities, showed increased qE compared to the wild type (WT) background and grew more slowly. The growth reduction was accompanied by increased accumulation of low-CO2-induced (LCI) proteins, suggesting that crkea3 mutants experience a relative CO2 deficit. Our data suggest that KEA3 activity modulates multiple regulatory layers of photosynthesis in unicellular green algae, extending beyond the functions previously described for vascular plants.

papers.title: Multi-scale three-dimensional visualization and analysis of barley anatomy using X-ray computed tomography
papers.abstract: Methods of determining plant anatomy often rely on time-consuming preparation techniques and targeted sampling of tissues of assumed importance. This typically involves single plane 2D examination over small profiles of sub-sampled plant tissue with limited ability for 3D extrapolation of internal anatomies of plant organs. This limitation can create phenotyping bottlenecks. These bottlenecks are particularly acute in plant species that are larger than commonly used model systems, which have typically been selected for their small size and suitability for high-density growth. Many major crop species, by contrast, are larger and have more complex internal structures. In this paper, we investigated whether X-ray computed tomography (XCT) provides an effective means of overcoming this phenotyping bottleneck, using the barley stem as a model system. Sample preparation approaches and scan parameters were compared. The resulting datasets were evaluated for qualitative observation and quantitative analyses of targeted volumetric structures. We demonstrate that plant samples suitable for XCT can be prepared without extended preparation times or toxic contrast agents. Freeze-drying provided cellular-resolution imaging of mature, structurally robust tissues, whereas critical point drying provided more reliable preservation of soft tissues undergoing active development. We then show how high-resolution scan data can be used to measure anatomical features in three dimensions, generate radial attenuation profiles, and extract computationally segmented models of isolated anatomical features. The scanning and analysis methods described here provide a means of recovering plant anatomy across multiple spatial scales in 3D digital reconstructions, providing routes to quantitative phenotyping in comparisons between different accessions, growth regimes, and mutants.

papers.title: Virtual Transcriptomics from Routine Histopathology Reveals Metastasis-Associated Programs and Molecular Risk States in Triple-Negative Breast Cancer
papers.abstract: Background: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is a highly aggressive and biologically heterogeneous disease for which reliable biomarkers of metastatic progression remain limited. Although transcriptomic profiling can reveal clinically important molecular programs, its routine implementation is constrained by cost, tissue availability, and workflow complexity. We hypothesized that metastasis-associated transcriptional states are encoded within routine hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) histopathology and can be recovered using artificial intelligence enabled virtual transcriptomics. Methods: We applied the Path2Space foundation model to infer genome-wide gene expression from treatment-naive TNBC H&E tissue microarrays and identified virtual transcriptomic programs associated with lymph node metastasis. We systematically validated candidate genes across three independent international TNBC cohorts (TCGA-BRCA, SCAN-B, and FUSCC). Candidate genes were evaluated in three independent international TNBC cohorts using experimentally measured RNA sequencing, followed by TNBC-specific co-expression network analysis, molecular subtype characterization, and cross-cohort meta-analysis. Results: Virtual transcriptomic analysis nominated 118 candidate genes associated with nodal status at a nominal discovery threshold; these candidates were subsequently evaluated using experimentally measured transcriptomic data across three independent international TNBC cohorts. Cross-cohort validation converged on a parsimonious two-gene Virtual Metastatic Prediction Score (VMPS) composed of TMEM184A and ZNF57, the only genes that remained significantly associated with nodal metastasis across all four datasets. TMEM184A and ZNF57 represented complementary biological programs: a TMEM184A-centered epithelial remodeling network and a ZNF57-centered KRAB zinc-finger transcriptional regulatory network. These transcriptional modules were biologically coherent and demonstrated reproducible associations with established TNBC molecular subtypes. Across TCGA-BRCA, SCAN-B, and FUSCC, the TMEM184A module showed a pooled OR of 1.44 per SD (95% CI, 1.25-1.67; I2=0%), while the two-gene VMPS showed a pooled OR of 1.58 (95% CI, 1.28-1.94). Moreover, higher VMPS and TMEM184A module activity defined reproducible metastatic risk gradients and enriched for lymph node-positive disease across independent cohorts. Conclusions: AI-enabled virtual transcriptomics transforms routine H&E histopathology into a scalable platform for molecular discovery in TNBC. These findings establish virtual transcriptomics as a scalable discovery framework for recovering biologically interpretable, metastasis associated molecular programs from routine histopathology, with potential applications in precision risk stratification.

papers.title: A small set of morphological metrics describes wing-planform plasticity: a correlational analysis in a population of the European grapevine moth Lobesia botrana (Lepidoptera: Tortricidae)
papers.abstract: The insect wing is a complex morpho-functional organ, and it remains unclear whether a set of well-defined metrics can fully capture wing-planform variation. To address this question, we digitised 339 male forewings of the European grapevine moth, Lobesia botrana (Lepidoptera: Tortricidae), an economically important grapevine pest. Specimens came from two non-overlapping seasonal flight generations. We applied two complementary shape-analysis methods - Generalised Procrustes Analysis (GPA) and Elliptic Fourier Analysis (EFA) - and correlated their principal components with four flight-related morphological metrics: aspect ratio (AR), a proxy for the second moment of wing area (MA), sweep angle (SA), and apex taper (Taper). For both methods, each of the first four principal components was most strongly correlated with its corresponding metric; together, these components represented 92.3% (GPA) and 95.7% (EFA) of the total variation of the shape. Both methods yielded concordant results, indicating that a small set of interpretable metrics captures the major axes of wing-planform variation. Generations differed significantly in mean MA, AR, and SA, and in Taper variance, consistent with seasonal phenotypic plasticity. These characters can be calculated from a small number of landmarks and therefore can serve as wing-shape markers. The analysis pipeline is implemented in the open-source MorphoGet software. This protocol provides an interpretable summary of wing-planform variation, applicable to flight-related morphology, ecology and evolution, pest monitoring, and other fields.

papers.title: Evolutionary dynamics with directed updating rules
papers.abstract: Evolutionary game theory describes how the frequencies of strategies change in a population when individuals imitate others who have higher payoffs. Models of imitation typically assume that updating is undirected, so that any individual may adopt the strategy of any other. But in many systems some replacements occur in one direction only: in a food chain, for example, a predator species can replace its prey but not the reverse. Here we study replicator dynamics with directed updating rules in a generalized Rock-Paper-Scissor game, in which each strategy can replace only one of the other two. Under undirected updating, increasing the payoff that Paper receives against Rock produces a population in which Scissors is close to fixation. Under directed updating, by contrast, the frequencies of all three strategies oscillate around an interior state. Moreover, when each strategy can replace only the strategy that beats it, increasing the payoff of Paper against Rock decreases the equilibrium frequency of Scissors, which is the opposite of its effect at the Nash equilibrium of the game. This reversal accompanies a reversal in the direction in which the population state rotates around the interior equilibrium. Our results indicate that the direction of strategy updating, and not only the payoff structure of the game, determines which strategies are common at equilibrium.

papers.title: A bacterial pathogen reveals a new mechanism of micron-scale nucleocytoplasmic transport
papers.abstract: In addition to its canonical role as a selective barrier, the nuclear envelope is increasingly recognized as a dynamic structure, remodeled to integrate mechanical cues. Here, we discover that the bacterial pathogen Rickettsia parkeri deforms the nuclear envelope to an unprecedented degree to invade and exit human cell nuclei through large membrane protrusions. This extreme envelope remodeling is tolerated in part due to a bacterial protein that associates with the nuclear membrane and promotes nuclear infection, along with a mechanosensitive host enzyme that releases a signaling molecule from deformed nuclei. These findings establish a new mechanism of nucleocytoplasmic transport that redefines the size limits of nuclear envelope deformation cells can tolerate and resolves a long-standing question of how micron-scale cargo, such as bacteria, enter nuclei.

papers.title: Characterization of Natural Killer Cell-Associated Prognostic Signature Reveals Immune Landscape and Prognostic Value in Uterine Corpus Endometrial Carcinoma (UCEC)
papers.abstract: Background: Natural killer (NK) cells are critical in eliminating virus-infected and cancer cells. Uterine corpus endometrial carcinoma (UCEC) is a common malignancy in women, and the role of NK cells in UCEC has attracted significant attention. This study aims to develop an NK cell-related gene signature (NRGs) to improve immunotherapy response and prognosis evaluation in UCEC. Methods: Consensus clustering classified UCEC samples based on NRGs. Univariate Cox regression, differential expression, and Lasso regression were used to build a prognostic model. Differences in tumor microenvironment (TME), immune checkpoints, and clinical features were compared between high- and low-risk groups. Results: High NK cell infiltration was associated with a favorable prognosis. Eleven key NRGs were identified, and consensus clustering divided patients into two clusters: Cluster 1 (C1) had better prognosis and higher immune cell infiltration. A nine-NRG signature (CEACAM1, IFNG, PTPN6, KNSTRN, XCL1, IL2RG, RAC3, MICB, CCL3) was developed. The high-risk group had more advanced-stage cases, higher-grade tumors, and serous carcinoma compared to the low-risk group (P < 0.05). Conclusions: The 9-NRGs signature demonstrates strong predictive performance and offers valuable insights for future immuno-oncology research.
